structure.title: Chapters 1–8 · A wager and a timetable
structure.text: A calculation at the Reform Club becomes a bet involving a substantial part of Fogg's fortune. Passepartout, who took the job hoping for a quiet life, has just enough time to pack a bag. A bank robbery gives somebody else a reason to study their route.

structure.title: Chapters 9–24 · India to the Pacific
structure.text: A railway line that exists on paper runs out on the ground. There are elephants to hire, steamers to catch and people whose urgent needs appear nowhere on the schedule. Time saved on one leg of the journey becomes something Fogg can spend on a stranger.

structure.title: Chapters 25–37 · America and the homeward crossing
structure.text: Trains and ships offer extraordinary speed and remain vulnerable to a blocked line, a captain's decision or the actions of a single passenger. The closer the travellers get to the club, the more a few missing hours seem to outweigh entire continents already crossed.

people.name: Phileas Fogg
people.text: Fogg's habits are so exact that a change in the temperature of his shaving water matters. His lack of visible excitement makes his spending instructive. Sometimes the first sign that he cares about somebody is the enormous price he is willing to pay.

people.name: Passepartout and Fix
people.text: Both interpret Fogg while travelling alongside him. The servant tries to fit the man's sudden eccentricities into a picture of an honourable employer. Fix takes the same reserve as evidence of a criminal with something to hide.

context.title: A world crossed on a ticket
context.text: The itinerary assumes regular departures, connecting ports, usable money and papers an official will recognise. Railways, shipping and imperial administration make that confidence possible. People working at the connections discover the gaps between a published timetable and an actual journey.

notice.text: Notice who looks out of the window.
notice.why: Fogg can cross remarkable country attending to cards or calculations. Passepartout and the narrator supply much of the sightseeing. That division makes it especially interesting when something outside the carriage finally claims Fogg's attention.

notice.text: Follow the money paid for an hour.
notice.why: Fogg buys speed, offers rewards and absorbs losses with the same composure. The sums show which delays can be overcome by wealth and which demand that somebody run a risk in person.

opening: Phileas Fogg's life runs so precisely that a disagreement at his club can become a timetable. He wagers a fortune that he can circle the world in eighty days and departs with a servant who had been hoping for a quiet position. Trains, steamships, and carefully calculated connections promise to make the journey possible. Weather, suspicion, and other people's emergencies have no obligation to cooperate. Verne turns the shrinking distances of the modern world into a chase in which stopping to help someone can cost everything.
